DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
This proposal raises the weekend rate from £145 to £165 and adds a two-night minimum for Saturday stays. It rests on three claims:
- last year's £10 increase showed weekend guests aren't price sensitive;
- the rate rise is worth at least £204,000 a year;
- the two-night minimum can only add to that.

Several parts are sound:
- **The competitor gap is real.** At £145 the hotel is £20–£35 below its set, so there is a reasonable case for a rise.
- **The occupancy arithmetic is correct.** The 2025 average of 79% checks out.
- **The value score is useful context.** It shows the hotel isn't currently overpriced.
- **The monitoring plan is a good start.** Weekly pick-up against last year is the right foundation.

However, the evidence on price sensitivity is confounded by the season. The revenue figure uses the wrong room count and applies the rise to rooms that won't pay it. And the two-night minimum conflicts directly with the wedding business described in the same document.

## 1. The June-to-July "test" measures the season, not the price

Occupancy rose from 81% to 89% in the month after the £10 increase. But section 2 itself says July and August are the strongest months, "driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays". Occupancy rose again in August, to 93%. The table shows a seasonal rise, and the price change happened to come just before it. The data can't show whether the higher rate had any effect, positive or negative.

The claim that the higher rate "reinforced our positioning" has no support. Better evidence would be:
- **Year-on-year occupancy** for July to December 2025 against the same months in 2024, at the old price.
- **Whether competitors' occupancy changed** over the same months.
- **Booking pace** for the weeks after the change.

## 2. The revenue figure uses 124 rooms; the hotel has 112

Section 2 says 112 rooms, but section 5's calculation uses 124. With the correct count:

112 × 104 nights × 79% × £20 ≈ **£184,000**, not £204,000.

## 3. Not all room-nights pay BAR

The £20 increase applies only to Best Available Rate bookings. Contracted corporate and group rates are honoured, and the document says weddings make up about 38% of Saturday room bookings, typically booked as blocks through the couple. Those rooms are likely on group rates, and the same may apply to some packages and corporate stays.

If Friday nights are mostly BAR and 38% of Saturdays aren't, the realistic figure is nearer **£150,000**, and possibly lower. The hotel's actual BAR share by night would settle it. Any online travel agent commission on the extra £20 should also be deducted.

## 4. Flat occupancy is an assumption, not a prudent one

Holding occupancy at 2025 levels while raising the rate 14% assumes guests don't respond to price at all. A cautious forecast would assume some loss. Break-even shows how much room there is:

- Revenue per available room now: £145 × 79% = £114.55
- At £165, occupancy can fall to about **69%** before weekend revenue is worse than today, a margin of about 10 points.

That margin is reasonable, and it is the honest way to present the risk. The 8.4 value-for-money score was earned at £145 and may fall at £165. The new price also matches the cheapest competitor rather than undercutting it, so after the change the hotel is no longer "priced well below" its set.

## 5. The two-night minimum works against the wedding business

Section 4 says wedding guests make up about 38% of Saturday bookings, and that they "arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning". That is a one-night stay including a Saturday, which the minimum would block. Contracted group blocks are honoured, but new weddings and individual wedding guests booking outside a block would have to buy two nights or go elsewhere. Quayside Hall's couples may also start recommending other hotels.

The minimum also has an uneven effect across the year:
- **On the 31 sell-out Saturdays,** demand exceeds rooms, so turning away one-night stays for two-night stays can add revenue.
- **On the other ~21 Saturdays,** a one-night booking turned away is probably just lost.

So the two-night minimum could reduce revenue, and £204,000 is not a "floor". A common approach is to apply minimum stays only on dates where demand is forecast to sell out. Wedding blocks should be explicitly exempt, and the hotel should talk to Quayside Hall before launch.

## 6. Monitoring

Monthly occupancy compared with 2025 will show a problem only after a month of lost bookings. Weekend leisure demand books well ahead, so **forward pace** (bookings on the books for future weekends, compared with last year) is the earlier warning. The weekly pick-up review should drive decisions, with a trigger defined on pace and not only on actual occupancy. A five-point fall is a sensible trigger, being about half the break-even margin.

## On the author's description

| Claim | What the document shows |
|---|---|
| The £10 rise led to higher occupancy | June to July is the seasonal peak (festival and school holidays) |
| £204,000 based on our trading history | Uses 124 rooms; the hotel has 112, so £184,000 before BAR adjustments |
| Assuming no occupancy change is "conservative" | It assumes zero price sensitivity |
| The two-night minimum makes £204,000 a "floor" | It blocks the one-night wedding stays that make up about 38% of Saturdays |
| Rates £20–£35 below competitors | True now; at £165 the hotel matches the cheapest |
| "We will see it within a month" | Forward pace would show it sooner |

## Recommendation

The rate rise is reasonable given the gap with competitors. The two-night minimum is risky as drafted. Before approval:
1. **Replace the June-to-July evidence** with a year-on-year and competitor comparison, or present the rise as a judgment call based on the competitor gap.
2. **Recalculate revenue with 112 rooms,** using only BAR room-nights, net of commission, and show the ~69% break-even.
3. **Limit the two-night minimum** to forecast sell-out dates, exempt wedding blocks, and agree the approach with Quayside Hall.
4. **Set a monitoring trigger on forward pace,** not only on monthly occupancy.
